releases.title: Agents join the vault, and apps start talking to each other
releases.summary: An agent is now a member of your vault with a name, its own permissions, and a record of everything it did. Apps expose their abilities to each other, so an action from one app shows up where you are working in another. Plus two new themes and a pass over every app.

body.text: An agent is no longer a hidden helper. It appears in your team with a name and a face, you grant it exactly what it may see and do, and it can be mentioned like anyone else.

text.text: Settings → Team lists every agent. Permissions are the same ones a person gets, and an agent with nothing granted says so plainly instead of failing quietly.
and its name in Chat. It answers in the thread, with the vault as context.
An agent never writes to your vault behind your back — changes arrive as a proposal you accept or discard.
One agent can delegate to another, and the second runs with the
of both their permissions — never more.
Put an agent on an automation.
Assign one as the assignee of an automation and it runs the work when the trigger fires.

body.text: See exactly what an agent did

text.text: panel: every run, every tool call, and every refusal, filterable by app, outcome, surface and period. It records metadata only — your prompts and the model's outputs are never stored.

body.text: Apps expose their abilities to each other
Until now each app was an island. An app can now publish typed actions that other apps discover and call — so a thing one app is good at becomes available in the place you are actually working.

text.text: In the ⋯ menu of any object
menu and block menu, alongside the built-in actions.
As a step in an automation
, and as something your agent can call on your behalf.

The first time an app runs another app's action, Brainstorm asks — and asks again if that action changes after you approved it. When one is refused, you get a named reason instead of a spinner that never stops.
— a flat paper-white light theme, no gradients, no glass.
— an entry you started typing the moment you opened a new day is now saved. Previously the first words could be dropped, and the day's body would then stay
on every later visit even though the word count still showed them.
A pass over all twenty apps
— the same faces for the same things: one control height, one chip, one empty state, one menu.

releases.title: Build an app inside Brainstorm, then install it
releases.summary: Write an app in the Code editor and install it into your own vault, with no build step and no terminal. Shared objects now show the people on them by name. Plus a security pass over sharing, and a fix for messages that went missing when you shared a channel.

text.text: An app here is two files: a
. That is the whole format, with no build step anywhere. Write those in the Code editor and Brainstorm will install them for you, straight out of your vault.
Select the code files that make up an app and choose Install as app. It lands on your dashboard right away, with no restart.
Install from a folder or a file
Point Brainstorm at a folder on disk, or at a
The agent can write the code
Ask it for an app and it drafts the files as cards you read and approve. Nothing reaches your vault until you say so, the same as everything else it proposes.
An app installed this way is unsigned, so it is marked as such and its actions are held to the sideloaded trust tier. It gets the capabilities you grant it and nothing more.
Everyone on a shared object now appears by name instead of a long
string. Names travel with the object itself, so there is no directory anywhere and the relay learns nothing new.
A name is only what someone calls themselves, so the key fingerprint sits beside it. Two people can never be told apart by a name alone.
Sharing a channel now brings every message
Some messages silently never arrived on the other side. They do now.
An invite code opens exactly one thing, once, and it expires. Revoking someone takes effect immediately.
A proposed file at a path you already have asks first
It used to quietly make a second copy.
The Code editor keeps still while you type
The right panel no longer blinks on every keystroke, and the file tree has folders.

body.text: After 0.4.3 turned on beta analytics, the shell and every app blocked Amplitude with a tight Content Security Policy. Events never left the device, and the console filled with CSP errors.

releases.title: Removing someone really removes them
releases.summary: When you take a collaborator off a shared note, page, or channel, they can no longer read anything you write afterward — access removal is now enforced by encryption, not just policy. Plus a PDF crash fix.

text.text: from a shared item, its encryption key is rotated and re-sealed for the people who remain. The removed person is left holding only the old key, so every edit you make
they're removed is unreadable to them — even if their app is still connected.
— remove someone while you're offline and the key rotation is queued, then completes automatically the moment you reconnect.
What they already saw, they keep.
Like every honest end-to-end encrypted system, removal is forward-looking: it stops future access — it can't un-send what already synced to their device.

Everything is encrypted per-entity on your devices; the sync relay only ever sees ciphertext, never your content or who you're working with.

One note on removing access: revoking a teammate stops future grants and hides the entity from them, but does not yet rotate the encryption key. A removed collaborator who already has the key can still read edits made after they're removed. Full rotate-on-revoke (new key, re-shared only with remaining members) is coming in a follow-up.
